detail:
A 2019 NIH-funded study by Kelly and Bridwell, published in the Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery, followed 286 adults ages 40–80 with lumbar curves of at least 30°. The nonoperative patients were treated with physical therapy, anti-inflammatory drugs, and injections delivering pain medication directly to nerve roots; they generally did not get worse over two years of follow-up. The study's authors describe the best guide for whether to operate as the extent of disability and how much symptoms interfere with daily life.

Mayo Clinic's overview describes the usual first steps for scoliosis pain care as physical therapy, stretching, dietary and nutrition changes, weight-bearing exercise, and treating co-existing osteoporosis. Surgery enters the picture if pain persists despite treatment or symptoms severely limit mobility.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about pain-management options appropriate for your situation.
sourceVideoTitle: For adult scoliosis, surgery, other treatments are viable options
summary: A 2019 NIH-funded study of 286 adults found nonoperative pain care (PT, anti-inflammatory drugs, nerve-root injections) generally did not worsen outcomes over two years.
takeaways: sources list the basics first: physical therapy, stretching, and weight bearing exercise
next steps sources name: medicines for pain and inflammation, and injections at the nerve root
people who stayed non surgical generally did not get worse over two years
surgery usually waits until pain persists or limits daily life; talk to your doctor
title: Stepwise non-surgical pain care
